scenes.narration: You've got all the pieces now.

This is where they fit together into one mental model you can carry into real code — plus an honest list of what the specification has already deprecated, so you don't build on the wrong thing. Learn MCP, on THE NBX STUDIO.

scenes.headline: The whole [machine]
scenes.caption: every part, at once
scenes.premise: Every piece of the protocol you've met, and the one question that tells them apart.
scenes.narration: Here's the whole thing on one screen. ^Tools are functions the model chooses, and Claude never runs them — your code does, in the loop. ^Resources are data your code fetches, and injecting one beats a tool call whenever you already know what's needed. ^Prompts are workflows a person triggers, which is how you ship your own expertise as a button. ^Sampling reverses the protocol so the client's key pays, which is what makes a public server affordable. ^Roots are file access control that the S D K hands you but never enforces. ^And notifications are how a slow tool proves it's alive. Underneath all six, one question keeps working: who is in control — and for sampling, who is paying.

scenes.caption: as of spec 2026-07-28
scenes.premise: Everything here still works today. Three of them are scheduled for removal, and the spec says not to start anything new on them.
scenes.narration: Before you go and build, here's the state of play, because a lot of MCP writing online predates it. ^Tools, resources and prompts are current, and they're the spine of everything. ^Elicitation is current, and it's where the protocol is putting its weight now. ^Sampling is deprecated as of the twenty twenty six revision — migrate to calling a provider API directly. ^Roots is deprecated too — pass paths as tool parameters, resource U R Is, or server config instead. ^And logging is deprecated — standard error on stdio, Open Telemetry in production. None of those three vanish tomorrow. They stay in the spec for at least twelve months and the code you inherit will be full of them, which is exactly why you learnt them. Just don't start something new on a feature the specification has already told you it's retiring.

scenes.narration: ^The final question, straight from the course. You're building a public MCP server for a weather service, users connect from their own apps, and the server needs a language model to write the forecast in plain English. What's the smartest approach? ^Put your Anthropic key on the server and call Claude directly. ^Or use sampling, so each client calls Claude with its own key. Have a think, and pause if you'd like a moment. ^Ready? Sampling. Option one works beautifully until the day somebody shares your server, and then every forecast in the world is billed to you — which is precisely the corner sampling was invented to avoid.
